content.intro: This lesson focuses on workflow reuse at scale. Workflow reuse at scale needs versioned interfaces, least privilege, compatibility tests, controlled rollout, and clear ownership of shared workflow libraries. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Workflow Reuse at Scale matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Workflow reuse at scale needs versioned interfaces, least privilege, compatibility tests, controlled rollout, and clear ownership of shared workflow libraries. Enterprise design requires consistent policy, explicit ownership, auditable privilege boundaries, reviewed shared workflows, controlled artifact promotion, and documented recovery.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Workflow reuse at scale needs versioned interfaces, least privilege, compatibility tests, controlled rollout, and clear ownership of shared workflow libraries. Enterprise design requires consistent policy, explicit ownership, auditable privilege boundaries, reviewed shared workflows, controlled artifact promotion, and documented recovery. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Shared workflow interfaces
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Input and output contracts
items.text: Write one step output as `name=value` to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, then declare job outputs if a downstream job needs the value. Use `$GITHUB_ENV` for values needed by later steps in the same job.

items.title: Versioned workflow dependencies
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Compatibility management
items.text: For compatibility management, state the expected input and result, identify the relevant workflow field or operational decision, and verify it with a controlled check plus run logs. Document the failure condition rather than relying on the YAML file merely parsing.

items.title: Workflow migration strategies
items.text: Use a temporary service with explicit port, test credentials, and readiness checks for CI. Production migrations need backward-compatibility, backup/recovery, and deployment-order planning.

items.title: Handling reusable workflow failures

name: Controlled workflow review
on: workflow_dispatch
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Review permissions, triggers, artifacts, and recovery evidence"

content_blocks.reset_steps: Remove temporary test workflows and never carry test credentials or sample outputs into production.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to workflow reuse at scale. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain workflow reuse at scale, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Standardize workflow behavior across teams without hiding important security boundaries.

content.task: Apply workflow reuse at scale to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Workflow reuse at scale needs versioned interfaces, least privilege, compatibility tests, controlled rollout, and clear ownership of shared workflow libraries.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Workflow reuse at scale needs versioned interfaces, least privilege, compatibility tests, controlled rollout, and clear ownership of shared workflow libraries. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Workflow reuse at scale needs versioned interfaces, least privilege, compatibility tests, controlled rollout, and clear ownership of shared workflow libraries.
Enterprise design requires consistent policy, explicit ownership, auditable privilege boundaries, reviewed shared workflows, controlled artifact promotion, and documented recovery.
